detail: A simulation driving the control points of the deformation curve, accounting for wind, high-energy dispersion, and thermal buoyancy [S1].

The claim states that the simulation drives the control points of the deformation curve and accounts for wind, high-energy dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly lists these three factors (wind, high-energy dispersion, and thermal buoyancy) as components of the velocity calculation for the particle simulation. Furthermore, the evidence describes a 'lattice in deformed world space' and mentions that the graphics hardware implicitly evaluates the 'deformation function D(P)', which implies that the simulation drives the deformation curve (represented by the lattice/control points). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
The velocity of a fire particle is determined by the sum of its base velocity, wind, dispersion, and buoyancy effects [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in Source [S1] that the particle simulation takes into account 'movement, wind, high-energy particle dispersion and thermal buoyancy.' Furthermore, Equation (7) in the source defines the velocity derivative as the sum of base velocity ($~v$), wind velocity ($~w$), dispersion velocity ($~d$), and buoyancy velocity ($~c$). Thus, all components mentioned in the claim are present in the evidence.

The parameters include: $T$ (temperature of the fire), $\vec{v}$ (velocity of the fire), $\vec{w}()$ (wind velocity as a function of position and time), $\vec{d}()$ (velocity attributed to high energy dispersion as a function of temperature), $\vec{c}()$ (velocity attributed to thermal buoyancy as a function of the temperature and particle age), $\beta$ (thermal expansion coefficient of an ideal gas, $= 1/T$), $g$ (gravitational constant), and $T_0$ (environment's ambient temperature, usually about 300K) [S1].
